# Cross-Validation in Practice

[Slides for this lecture](15-cv-in-practice_slides.html)

```{r packages}
#| include: false
library("tidyverse")
theme_set(theme_bw())
set.seed(20261015)

# Fixed decimals with thousands separators, and percentages, for prose.
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, digits), "%")
# "a", "a and b", "a, b, and c".
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 1) x else if (length(x) == 2) paste(x, collapse = " and ") else
    paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), ", and ", x[length(x)])
}
dollars <- function(v) {
  ifelse(is.na(v), NA,
         paste0("$", format(v, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)))
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### Learning objectives
After this lecture you should be able to

- **explain** why the smallest cross-validation estimate among many candidate
models tends to underestimate the test error of the model it selects, and
**predict** how that optimism changes with the number of candidates, the
noise in their estimates, and the correlation between them,
- **describe** a workflow that keeps test data out of every choice: split off
the test data first; choose by cross-validation on the training data only,
with every data-dependent step of fitting (here, standardization) repeated
inside each fold and the features and tuning parameters chosen by comparing
the cross-validation estimates; refit the chosen model to all the training
data; and evaluate it once on the test data,
- **classify** the data used at each step of an analysis as training,
validation, or test data, and **identify** which choices used which, and
- **explain** why test data that have been used to choose among models no
longer give an honest estimate of the chosen model's test error.
:::

## Ames home sales

**Question.** How accurately can the sale price of a home in Ames, Iowa, be
predicted from its size, age, and location, and which model should make the
predictions?

**Data.** `modeldata::ames` records `r format(nrow(modeldata::ames), big.mark = ",")`
home sales in Ames from `r min(modeldata::ames$Year_Sold)` to
`r max(modeldata::ames$Year_Sold)`. The response is the sale price,
`Sale_Price`, analyzed as $\log_{10}$ of the price in dollars: prices are
right-skewed, and an error on the $\log_{10}$ scale is a relative error, so a
\$20,000 miss counts more on a \$100,000 home than on a \$400,000 one. The
explanatory variables are, in this order, above-ground living area
(`Gr_Liv_Area`), year built (`Year_Built`), basement area
(`Total_Bsmt_SF`), garage area (`Garage_Area`), and the home's `Longitude`
and `Latitude`. The tabs plot the sale price against living area, against
each of the six explanatory variables, and on a map.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r ames-data}
#| output: false
homes <- modeldata::ames |>
  mutate(log_price = log10(Sale_Price))
n_homes <- nrow(homes)

explanatory <- c(Gr_Liv_Area = "Living area (sq ft)", Year_Built = "Year built",
                 Total_Bsmt_SF = "Basement area (sq ft)",
                 Garage_Area = "Garage area (sq ft)",
                 Longitude = "Longitude", Latitude = "Latitude")
vars <- names(explanatory)
big_area <- 4000
n_big <- sum(homes$Gr_Liv_Area > big_area)

price_axis <- scale_y_log10(breaks = c(25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800) * 1000,
                            labels = dollars)
living_plot <- ggplot(homes, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  price_axis +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Sale price (log scale)",
       title = "modeldata::ames")
six_plot <- homes |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(vars), names_to = "variable") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(explanatory[variable], levels = explanatory)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  price_axis +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Sale price (log scale)", title = "modeldata::ames")
map_plot <- ggplot(arrange(homes, Sale_Price),
                   aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = dollars,
                        breaks = c(50, 100, 200, 400) * 1000) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(color = "Sale price", title = "modeldata::ames")
```

On the log scale, price rises roughly linearly with living area, with a few
exceptions: `r n_big` homes have more than `r format(big_area, big.mark = ",")`
square feet, and some of them sold for far less than the trend. Newer homes,
and homes with larger basements and garages, also sell for more; the vertical
stripe at zero basement area is the homes without a basement. On the map,
the most expensive homes are in the north of the city and the least expensive
in its center and east, so nearby homes sell for similar prices.

## Candidate models

```{r training-sample}
m <- 200
one_id <- sample(n_homes, m)
show_K <- c(1, 15, 40)
```

A training sample of `r m` homes, drawn at random from the `r format(n_homes, big.mark = ",")`,
will be used to choose a model. The first tab shows it (black) against the
other `r format(n_homes - m, big.mark = ",")` homes (grey). The other tabs add
KNN fits that use living area only, with $K$ = `r and_list(show_K)` neighbors.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r knn-function}
#| output: false
# Predictions of KNN regression on the first q explanatory variables, for
# every K in K_values. The explanatory variables are standardized with the
# means and standard deviations of `fit`, so standardization is part of the
# fit.
knn_predict <- function(fit, new, q, K_values) {
  x_names <- vars[seq_len(q)]
  center <- colMeans(fit[x_names])
  spread <- map_dbl(fit[x_names], sd)
  x_fit <- scale(as.matrix(fit[x_names]), center, spread)
  x_new <- scale(as.matrix(new[x_names]), center, spread)
  # Squared Euclidean distances: one row per home in `new`.
  dist2 <- outer(rowSums(x_new^2), rowSums(x_fit^2), "+") - 2 * x_new %*% t(x_fit)
  K_max <- max(K_values)
  nearest <- t(apply(dist2, 1, \(d) order(d)[seq_len(K_max)]))
  y_near <- matrix(fit$log_price[nearest], nrow(new))
  # Column K is the average response of the K nearest training homes.
  running_mean <- t(apply(y_near, 1, cumsum)) / rep(seq_len(K_max), each = nrow(new))
  running_mean[, K_values, drop = FALSE]
}
```

```{r knn-one-feature}
#| output: false
one_train <- homes[one_id, ]
K_labels <- paste("K =", show_K)
area_grid <- tibble(Gr_Liv_Area = seq(min(homes$Gr_Liv_Area),
                                      max(homes$Gr_Liv_Area), length.out = 500))
knn_matrix <- knn_predict(one_train, area_grid, q = 1, K_values = show_K)
colnames(knn_matrix) <- K_labels
knn_curves <- as_tibble(knn_matrix) |>
  bind_cols(area_grid) |>
  pivot_longer(-Gr_Liv_Area, names_to = "K", values_to = "log_price") |>
  mutate(K = factor(K, levels = K_labels), Sale_Price = 10^log_price)

sample_base <- ggplot(homes, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = Sale_Price)) +
  geom_point(data = homes[-one_id, ], color = "grey80", size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = one_train, size = 1.2) +
  price_axis +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Sale price (log scale)",
       title = paste(m, "training homes (black) and the other",
                     format(n_homes - m, big.mark = ","), "(grey)"))
add_knn <- function(through) {
  sample_base +
    geom_line(data = filter(knn_curves, as.integer(K) <= through),
              aes(color = K, linetype = K), linewidth = 0.9) +
    scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73"), K_labels)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = setNames(c("solid", "dashed", "dotdash"), K_labels)) +
    labs(color = "Living area only", linetype = "Living area only")
}
knn_plots <- map(seq_along(show_K), add_knn)
```

The training homes cover most of the range of living area but miss the
largest homes. With $K = `r show_K[1]`$ the fit jumps from one training
home's price to the next; with $K = `r show_K[2]`$ and $K = `r show_K[3]`$ it
follows the trend more smoothly. All three fits are flat beyond the largest
training home, at the geometric mean price (the average on the $\log_{10}$
scale) of its nearest neighbors.

### Nested KNN candidates

The candidates are KNN regressions that differ in two tuning parameters: how
many of the six explanatory variables they use, and how many neighbors. For a
home with explanatory variables $x_0$,

$$\hat f_{q,K}(x_0) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_{q,K}(x_0)} y_i,$$

where

- $y_i = \log_{10}\left(\texttt{Sale\_Price}_i\right)$ is the response of
training home $i$,
- $p = `r length(vars)`$ is the number of explanatory variables available,
- $q = 1, \ldots, p$ is the number used, always the first $q$ in the order
listed above, so $q = 1$ is living area alone and $q = p$ adds year built,
basement area, garage area, longitude, and latitude,
- the features are those $q$ explanatory variables, each standardized with
the mean and standard deviation of the training homes,
- $\mathcal{N}_{q,K}(x_0)$ is the set of the $K$ training homes closest to
$x_0$ in Euclidean distance on the (standardized) features, and
- $K$ is the number of neighbors.

```{r candidates}
q_values <- seq_along(vars)
K_grid <- 1:40
candidates <- expand_grid(q = q_values, K = K_grid)
S <- nrow(candidates)
n_folds <- 10
```

With $K = `r min(K_grid)`, \ldots, `r max(K_grid)`$ and
$q = `r min(q_values)`, \ldots, `r max(q_values)`$ there are $S = `r S`$
candidate models, indexed $s = 1, \ldots, S$. The order of the explanatory
variables was chosen without using the response. Ordering them by their
correlation with price in the data at hand would be another data-dependent
step, and would have to be repeated inside every fold.

### Candidate cross-validation

The function below computes the $k$-fold cross-validation estimate
$\text{CV}_{(k)}$ of the test MSE, on the $\log_{10}$ scale, with
$k = `r n_folds`$, for all `r S` candidates at once. The number of folds $k$
is unrelated to the number of neighbors $K$.

Because `knn_predict()` standardizes with the training folds only,
standardization happens inside the folds. The choice of $q$ and $K$ does not:
every candidate is fit and evaluated in every fold, and $q$ and $K$ are chosen
afterward by comparing the `r S` cross-validation estimates. Both steps use
the training data only.

```{r cv-function}
predict_candidates <- function(fit, new) {
  do.call(cbind, map(q_values, \(q) knn_predict(fit, new, q, K_grid)))
}
cv_mse <- function(data, fold) {
  predicted <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(data), S)
  for (l in unique(fold)) {
    held_out <- fold == l
    predicted[held_out, ] <- predict_candidates(data[!held_out, ], data[held_out, ])
  }
  colMeans((data$log_price - predicted)^2)
}
```

## Selection optimism

### One training sample

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r one-sample-errors}
#| output: false
# CV estimate on the training homes and MSE on all other homes, for every
# candidate.
sample_errors <- function(train_id) {
  train <- homes[train_id, ]
  rest <- homes[-train_id, ]
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = length(train_id)))
  mutate(candidates,
         cv = cv_mse(train, fold),
         test = colMeans((rest$log_price - predict_candidates(train, rest))^2))
}
one_errors <- sample_errors(one_id)
one_best <- slice_min(one_errors, cv, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
one_oracle <- slice_min(one_errors, test, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
# Candidates whose MSE on the other homes is within 5% of the smallest.
near_share <- 0.05
n_near_oracle <- sum(one_errors$test <= (1 + near_share) * one_oracle$test)
```

```{r one-sample-plots}
#| output: false
q_labels <- paste0("q = ", q_values, ": ", c("living area", "+ year built",
                   "+ basement", "+ garage", "+ longitude", "+ latitude"))
error_labels <- c("10-fold CV (training homes)", "MSE on the other homes")
one_long <- one_errors |>
  pivot_longer(c(cv, test), names_to = "error", values_to = "mse") |>
  mutate(error = factor(if_else(error == "cv", error_labels[1], error_labels[2]),
                        levels = error_labels),
         q = factor(q_labels[q], levels = q_labels))
one_marked <- one_best |>
  pivot_longer(c(cv, test), names_to = "error", values_to = "mse") |>
  mutate(error = factor(if_else(error == "cv", error_labels[1], error_labels[2]),
                        levels = error_labels),
         q = factor(q_labels[q], levels = q_labels))

curve_plot <- function(show) {
  ggplot(filter(one_long, error %in% show),
         aes(x = 1 / K, y = mse, color = error, linetype = error, shape = error)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(data = filter(one_marked, error %in% show), size = 3) +
    facet_wrap(~ q, nrow = 2) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = 1 / c(1, 5, 40), labels = c("1", "1/5", "1/40")) +
    scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("#D55E00", "#0072B2"), error_labels),
                       drop = FALSE) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = setNames(c("solid", "dashed"), error_labels),
                          drop = FALSE) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = setNames(c(17, 16), error_labels), drop = FALSE) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = range(one_long$mse)) +
    labs(x = "Flexibility 1/K (log scale)", y = "MSE of log10 price",
         color = NULL, linetype = NULL, shape = NULL,
         title = paste("One sample of", m, "homes; the point marks the smallest CV estimate")) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
one_cv_plot <- curve_plot(error_labels[1])
one_both_plot <- curve_plot(error_labels)
```
:::

For the `r m` training homes plotted earlier, the first tab plots the
`r n_folds`-fold cross-validation estimate of every candidate against the
flexibility $1/K$, one panel per $q$. The remaining
`r format(n_homes - m, big.mark = ",")` homes were never used to fit or to
choose, so they are test data for this sample; the second tab adds each
candidate's MSE on them.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Cross-validation
```{r one-cv-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.2
one_cv_plot
```

#### + Other homes
```{r one-both-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.2
one_both_plot
```
:::

Cross-validation chooses $q = `r one_best$q`$ and $K = `r one_best$K`$, with
an estimated MSE of `r fmt(one_best$cv, 5)`. Fit to the same `r m` homes, that
model's MSE on the other homes is `r fmt(one_best$test, 5)`,
`r if (one_best$cv < one_best$test) paste(pct((one_best$test - one_best$cv) / one_best$cv), "above its cross-validation estimate") else paste(pct((one_best$cv - one_best$test) / one_best$cv), "below its cross-validation estimate")`.
The candidate with the smallest MSE on the other homes is $q = `r one_oracle$q`$,
$K = `r one_oracle$K`$, at `r fmt(one_oracle$test, 5)`. In every panel the two
curves have similar shapes, and many candidates have nearly the same MSE on
the other homes: `r n_near_oracle` of the `r S` are within
`r pct(near_share, 0)` of the smallest. In this sample the cross-validation
estimate is above the MSE on the other homes for
`r pct(mean(one_errors$cv > one_errors$test), 0)` of the candidates; the
minimum falls where the cross-validation curve dips toward the other curve.

### Noisy minimum

The same training homes chose the model and estimated its error. For a
candidate $s$ fixed in advance,

$$\text{CV}_s = \text{MSE}^{\text{test}}_s + e_s,$$

where

- $\text{CV}_s$ is the $k$-fold cross-validation estimate for candidate $s$,
- $\text{MSE}^{\text{test}}_s$ is the test MSE of candidate $s$ fit to all
the training homes, and
- $e_s$ is the estimation error, which averages close to zero over repeated
training samples (slightly above zero, since each fit in cross-validation uses
$(k - 1)/k$ of the homes).

The selected candidate is $\hat s$, the one with the smallest $\text{CV}_s$,
and its reported estimate is $\text{CV}_{\hat s} = \min_s \text{CV}_s$. Among
candidates whose test MSEs are nearly equal, the one with the most negative
$e_s$ wins, so $e_{\hat s}$ tends to be negative even though no fixed $e_s$
is.

Two candidates with equal test MSE show the size of the effect. Suppose
$e_1$ and $e_2$ are jointly normal, each $N\left(0, \tau^2\right)$, with
correlation $\rho$.
Since $\min(a, b) = (a + b)/2 - |a - b|/2$ and
$e_1 - e_2 \sim N\left[0, 2\tau^2(1 - \rho)\right]$, whose absolute value has
mean $\sqrt{2\tau^2(1 - \rho)}\sqrt{2/\pi} = 2\tau\sqrt{(1 - \rho)/\pi}$,

$$E\left[\min\left(e_1, e_2\right)\right] = \frac{E\left[e_1\right] + E\left[e_2\right]}{2} - \frac{E\left[\left|e_1 - e_2\right|\right]}{2} = -\tau\sqrt{\frac{1 - \rho}{\pi}},$$

where $\tau$ is the standard deviation of each estimation error and $\rho$ the
correlation between them. The optimism grows with the noise $\tau$, which is
larger for smaller training samples; it shrinks as the estimates become more
correlated, vanishing when $\rho = 1$; and it grows with the number of
near-tied candidates, since the minimum of more noisy values is lower.

### Repeated samples

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r optimism-simulation}
#| output: false
n_reps <- 300
# The QDA lecture's rule of thumb: the smallest odd integer above sqrt(n).
odd_above_sqrt <- function(n) {
  k <- floor(sqrt(n))
  if (k %% 2 == 0) k + 1 else k + 2
}
K_rule <- odd_above_sqrt(m)
procedure_labels <- c(
  paste0("Rule of thumb: q = ", max(q_values), ", K = ", K_rule, "\n(1 candidate)"),
  paste0("Best K, q = ", max(q_values), "\n(", length(K_grid), " candidates)"),
  paste0("Best K and q\n(", S, " candidates)"))
summarize_sample <- function(errors) {
  rule <- which(errors$q == max(q_values) & errors$K == K_rule)
  all_six <- which(errors$q == max(q_values))
  best_K <- all_six[which.min(errors$cv[all_six])]
  best_all <- which.min(errors$cv)
  chosen <- c(rule, best_K, best_all)
  tibble(procedure = procedure_labels, q = errors$q[chosen], K = errors$K[chosen],
         cv = errors$cv[chosen], test = errors$test[chosen])
}
optimism <- map(seq_len(n_reps), \(r) {
  summarize_sample(sample_errors(sample(n_homes, m))) |> mutate(rep = r)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(procedure = factor(procedure, levels = procedure_labels),
         gap = cv - test,
         relative_gap = gap / test)
optimism_summary <- optimism |>
  group_by(procedure) |>
  summarize(mean_gap = mean(gap), mean_relative = mean(relative_gap),
            se_relative = sd(relative_gap) / sqrt(n()),
            share_below = mean(gap < 0), mean_test = mean(test),
            .groups = "drop")
opt_of <- function(i, col) optimism_summary[[col]][i]
# "x% below" or "x% above" for the average relative gap of procedure i.
gap_text <- function(i) {
  g <- opt_of(i, "mean_relative")
  paste(pct(abs(g)), if (g < 0) "below" else "above")
}

optimism_plot <- ggplot(optimism, aes(x = procedure, y = 100 * relative_gap)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey90", scale = "width", quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
              quantile.linetype = "solid") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3,
               fill = "#E69F00") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "CV estimate minus test MSE\n(% of test MSE)",
       title = paste(n_reps, "training samples of", m, "homes"),
       caption = "Lines = quartiles and median, diamond = mean, dashed line = no gap.")
```
:::

One sample can be lucky or unlucky. To see what happens on average, a
training sample of `r m` homes was drawn `r n_reps` times. In each sample,
three procedures chose a model by `r n_folds`-fold cross-validation, and the
chosen model's cross-validation estimate was compared with its MSE on the
other `r format(n_homes - m, big.mark = ",")` homes:

- **rule of thumb**: one candidate fixed in advance, all six explanatory
variables with $K = `r K_rule`$, the smallest odd integer above
$\sqrt{`r m`}$ (the QDA lecture's rule of thumb), so nothing is chosen,
- **best $K$**: the smallest estimate among the `r length(K_grid)` values of
$K$ with all six explanatory variables, and
- **best $K$ and $q$**: the smallest estimate among all `r S` candidates.

The figure shows, for each procedure, the distribution over samples of the gap
between the chosen model's cross-validation estimate and its test MSE, as a
percentage of the test MSE. A negative gap means the estimate was too
optimistic.

```{r optimism-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
optimism_plot
```

For the rule of thumb, which chooses nothing, the cross-validation estimate
averages `r gap_text(1)` the test MSE (simulation standard error
`r fmt(100 * opt_of(1, "se_relative"), 1)` percentage points) and falls below
it in `r pct(opt_of(1, "share_below"), 0)` of samples. The best of
`r length(K_grid)` values of $K$ averages `r gap_text(2)`, and the best of all
`r S` candidates `r gap_text(3)` (standard error
`r fmt(100 * opt_of(3, "se_relative"), 1)` percentage points), below the test
MSE in `r pct(opt_of(3, "share_below"), 0)` of samples.

The choosing also gains something real: the average test MSE of the model
chosen from all `r S` candidates is `r fmt(opt_of(3, "mean_test"), 5)`,
against `r fmt(opt_of(1, "mean_test"), 5)` for the rule of thumb.
On these data the optimism is modest. By the two-candidate
calculation above, it would be larger with smaller training samples, whose
estimates are noisier, or with more near-tied candidates whose estimates are
less correlated.

## Test data workflow

```{r final-split}
test_share <- 0.2
test_id <- sample(n_homes, round(test_share * n_homes))
train <- homes[-test_id, ]
test <- homes[test_id, ]
```

In practice there is one data set, not a population to resample from. The
figure splits the `r format(n_homes, big.mark = ",")` homes at random into
`r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` training homes (blue circles) and
`r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test homes (orange triangles),
`r pct(test_share, 0)` of the total.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r final-split-plot}
#| output: false
set_labels <- c("Training", "Test")
split_plot <- homes |>
  mutate(set = factor(if_else(row_number() %in% test_id, "Test", "Training"),
                      levels = set_labels)) |>
  arrange(set) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = Sale_Price, color = set, shape = set)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Training = "#0072B2", Test = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Training = 16, Test = 17)) +
  price_axis +
  labs(x = "Living area (sq ft)", y = "Sale price (log scale)", color = NULL,
       shape = NULL, title = "modeldata::ames, one random split")
```
:::

```{r final-split-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
split_plot
```

The two sets overlap over the bulk of the data. Of the `r n_big` homes with
more than `r format(big_area, big.mark = ",")` square feet, `r sum(test$Gr_Liv_Area > big_area)`
`r if (sum(test$Gr_Liv_Area > big_area) == 1) "is" else "are"` in the test set.

### Workflow steps

The simulation shows that when the same data choose a model and estimate its
error, the estimate is optimistic on average. The remedy is to keep some data
out of the choosing entirely:

1. **Split off test data first**, at random, before any plotting, fitting, or
choosing.
2. **Choose by cross-validation on the training data only.** Every
data-dependent step of fitting is repeated inside each fold using only the
training folds: here standardization, computed inside `knn_predict()`. The
held-out folds are validation sets. Feature selection (the number $q$ of
explanatory variables) and tuning ($K$) are done by comparing the
cross-validation estimates of all the candidates, so they also use the
training data only, and the smallest estimate tends to be optimistic.
3. **Refit the chosen model to all the training data.**
4. **Evaluate it once on the test data**, and report that test MSE as the
estimate of its error on new homes.

### Choosing

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r final-cv}
#| output: false
train_fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = nrow(train)))
final_errors <- mutate(candidates, cv = cv_mse(train, train_fold))
final_best <- slice_min(final_errors, cv, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
final_min_by_q <- final_errors |>
  group_by(q) |>
  summarize(cv = min(cv), .groups = "drop")

final_cv_plot <- final_errors |>
  mutate(q = factor(q_labels[q], levels = q_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = 1 / K, y = cv)) +
  geom_line(color = "#D55E00") +
  geom_point(data = mutate(final_best, q = factor(q_labels[q], levels = q_labels)),
             color = "#D55E00", shape = 17, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ q, nrow = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = 1 / c(1, 5, 40), labels = c("1", "1/5", "1/40")) +
  labs(x = "Flexibility 1/K (log scale)", y = "10-fold CV estimate of MSE\n(log10 price)",
       title = paste(format(nrow(train), big.mark = ","),
                     "training homes; the triangle marks the minimum"))
```
:::

The figure plots the `r n_folds`-fold cross-validation estimate of each of
the `r S` candidates on the `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` training
homes.

```{r final-cv-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
final_cv_plot
```

With `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` training homes the curves are
smoother than for the sample of `r m`. Each curve rises steeply toward
$K = 1$. The smallest estimate in each panel is
`r and_list(fmt(final_min_by_q$cv, 4))` for $q = 1$ through
`r max(q_values)`: year built gives by far the largest improvement and
basement area the next largest, while the last three explanatory variables
lower it only slightly. Cross-validation chooses $q = `r final_best$q`$ and
$K = `r final_best$K`$, with an estimated MSE of `r fmt(final_best$cv, 5)`.

### Final evaluation

```{r final-test}
final_pred <- knn_predict(train, test, final_best$q, final_best$K)
final_test_mse <- mean((test$log_price - final_pred)^2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r final-test-big}
#| output: false
test_errors <- test$log_price - final_pred
test_big <- test$Gr_Liv_Area > big_area
final_test_mse_small <- mean(test_errors[!test_big]^2)
big_pred_price <- 10^final_pred[test_big]
big_price <- test$Sale_Price[test_big]
# Standard error of the test MSE, a mean of nrow(test) squared errors.
final_test_se <- sd(test_errors^2) / sqrt(nrow(test))
# Share of test homes predicted within the root-mean-square factor.
final_rmse <- sqrt(final_test_mse)
within_rmse <- mean(abs(test_errors) < final_rmse)
# For illustration only, outside the workflow: every candidate's test MSE.
hindsight <- mutate(final_errors,
                    test = colMeans((test$log_price - predict_candidates(train, test))^2))
hindsight_best <- slice_min(hindsight, test, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
# Relative gap between the test MSE and the CV estimate, as a % of the CV estimate.
rel_gap <- function(test_mse, cv) {
  paste(pct(abs(test_mse / cv - 1), 0), if (test_mse > cv) "above" else "below")
}
```
:::

Refit to all `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` training homes and used
once on the `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test homes, the chosen
model has a test MSE of `r fmt(final_test_mse, 5)`, against its
cross-validation estimate of `r fmt(final_best$cv, 5)`. The root mean squared
error is `r fmt(final_rmse, 3)` on the $\log_{10}$ scale. An error of $e$ on
that scale is a factor of $10^e$ in price, so the root-mean-square error is a
factor of
$10^{`r fmt(final_rmse, 3)`} = `r fmt(10^final_rmse, 2)`$, too high or too
low; `r pct(within_rmse, 0)` of the test homes are predicted within that
factor.

The test MSE is `r rel_gap(final_test_mse, final_best$cv)` the
cross-validation estimate. Selection optimism is at most a modest part of
this gap. In the simulation, the smallest of `r S` estimates averaged
`r gap_text(3)` the test MSE with `r m` training homes; with
`r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` training homes each estimate is less
noisy, so the optimism should be smaller. Choosing differently would not have
closed the gap either: for illustration only, outside the workflow, the
candidate with the smallest MSE on these test homes, $q = `r hindsight_best$q`$
and $K = `r hindsight_best$K`$, has a test MSE only
`r pct(1 - hindsight_best$test / final_test_mse)` below the chosen model's.

Part of the gap comes from the `r sum(test_big)` test
`r if (sum(test_big) == 1) "home" else "homes"` with more than
`r format(big_area, big.mark = ",")` square feet, which sold for
`r and_list(dollars(round(big_price, -3)))` and
`r if (sum(test_big) == 1) "was" else "were"` predicted at
`r and_list(dollars(round(big_pred_price, -3)))`, the geometric mean price
(the average on the $\log_{10}$ scale) of the nearest training homes; without
`r if (sum(test_big) == 1) "it" else "them"` the test MSE is
`r fmt(final_test_mse_small, 5)`, `r rel_gap(final_test_mse_small, final_best$cv)`
the cross-validation estimate. The standard error of a mean of
`r nrow(test)` squared errors is `r fmt(final_test_se, 5)`,
`r pct(final_test_se / final_test_mse, 0)` of the test MSE, so the gap is
`r if (abs(final_test_mse / final_best$cv - 1) < final_test_se / final_test_mse) "smaller" else "larger"`
than the variability of an MSE computed from `r nrow(test)` homes. The test MSE is
the number to report: no choice was made with the test homes, so the
selection optimism of the previous section does not affect it.

The test data can be used only once: if the test MSE were used to choose
again, for example by going back to try another $q$ after seeing it, the test
homes would become one more validation set, and the reported error would be
the minimum over the choices tried, with the same optimism as the minimum of
the cross-validation curve.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Beyond this course
- **One-standard-error rule.** When the cross-validation curve is flat near
its minimum, as in several panels above, choose the simplest candidate (the
largest $K$, or the smallest $q$) whose estimate is within one standard error
of the minimum. It trades a little estimated error for a model less tuned to
the noise in this particular sample.
- **Nested cross-validation.** When the data are too few to set aside test
data, an outer cross-validation loop around the whole procedure ("choose $q$
and $K$ by inner cross-validation, then refit") estimates the test error of
that procedure, using every observation for both choosing and testing, but
never in the same loop.
:::

## Activity

In small groups, work through `15-cv-in-practice_activity.R`
([download](15-cv-in-practice_activity.R)) in RStudio. It uses
`modeldata::stackoverflow`, responses from `r format(nrow(modeldata::stackoverflow), big.mark = ",")`
developers to Stack Overflow's annual Developer Survey, to ask which
developers work remotely; the response variable is `Remote`, whether or not
the developer works remotely. Your group splits off test data, looks at the
training data, compares logistic regression, LDA, and KNN with several values
of $K$ by 10-fold cross-validation on the training data, chooses one, and
evaluates it once on the test data. The classifiers are compared mainly by
the area under the ROC curve (AUC) and also by the error rate, each against
the benchmark of always predicting "Not remote," whose AUC is 0.5. Most of
the code is provided; the discussion questions at the end of the script are
the point of the activity.

## Conclusion

Cross-validation estimates the test error of a model fixed in advance with
little bias. Once it is used to choose among candidate models, its minimum is
no longer such an estimate. The same data choose the model and estimate its
error, so the candidate that wins is the one whose estimate happened to fall
lowest, and the winning estimate tends to be below the chosen model's test
error. The optimism grows with the number of nearly equivalent candidates and
with the noise in their estimates, and shrinks when the estimates are
strongly correlated.

The remedy is a division of labor among the three roles of data. Test data
are split off first and set aside. All choosing happens by cross-validation on
the training data only. Every data-dependent step of fitting, such as
standardization, is repeated inside each fold, so that the held-out folds
serve as validation sets; features and tuning parameters are then chosen by
comparing the cross-validation estimates of the candidates, and the smallest
of those estimates tends to be optimistic. The chosen model is refit to all the
training data and evaluated once on the test data, and that test error is
what gets reported. Using the test data to choose again turns them into
validation data and brings the optimism back.

The next lecture begins Chapter 6, linear model selection and regularization,
with subset selection. The bootstrap chapter that follows this one in the
book is optional reading.
